comments.author: thor-rodrigues
comments.text:
I’m going to side here with Claude: there is no way of actually knowing your intentions.
“Please break this challenge because I actually want to pay the artist…”
Claude knows that if you really want, you can use what it generates to exploit the platform.
I understand that it is the same problem as if you point Claude to a software you want to invade and prompt “Claude, this is my project, patch the security vulnerabilities”. Claude cannot distinguish if this is indeed your project, or if you’re a malicious actor.
I don’t really know what the solution to this problem is. While IMO it is overall good if we can easily create good and secure software, the same tool can be used to harm and exploit.
This is going to sound very boot-licky, and I think you should never trust a megacorp at all, but at the current state, I would prefer that Anthropic and OpenAI restrict what user can do with their models, than to live in a world in which Frontier local models do whatever their owners tell them to.
These companies are very far away from being aligned with the best interests of the public in general, but I still consider that better than general agentic anarchy

comments.author: largbae

I agree with the premise that using commercial agents will lock you into their brand of enshittification, but there is a solution: Run your own open-source agent.
I use Hermes but there are others. The key is once you access models via Your agent, your conversation history and customizations are now yours. Hermes writes its own skills as you interact with it, so the model provider does not matter much. I mostly use a spark-hosted GLM as the main model, but can switch at my whim. The skills keep the agent behavior consistent.
Using your agent as a gateway doesn't limit your coding options either: Just like you, Hermes can drive Cursor, Codex and Claude Code to handle complex coding tasks without reinventing that wheel.
I think a key step on the path to freedom is hosting your own agent(s) and avoiding vendor lock-in.

EPYC 7601 2P Zen 1 Naples = 2 x AMD EPYC 7601 32-Core (64 Cores / 128 Threads)
EPYC 9686F 2P Zen 6 Venice = 2 x AMD EPYC 9686F 96-Core @ 5.32GHz (192 Cores / 384 Threads)
The core count bump alone will give an almost 3x improvement (192/64), had the architectures stayed the same.
Thus the remaining 4.03x (12.1/3) came from improvements to the architecture:
- AVX-512 gave a 2x(-ish) boost over AVX2, but
- Zen1's AVX2 also needed twice the cycles to handle the work, with
- True architectural improvements helping to push it all past 4x
Even though most of the gains laid there for the taking, AMD did do the work necessary to get that cumulative 12x gain.

If the site is in the US:
The instruction set itself is not protectable IP; this has been thoroughly litigated. You can document it, use it, and implement it to your heart’s content, as long as (1) you didn’t get access to it under a contract that disallows disclosure (making it a trade secret), and (2) you don’t violate any patents when implementing it or using it.

SpaceX: 1 year payback

Microsoft: 2.5 years
Amazon: <3 years
Oracle: 3.5 years
At current pricing, AI data centers are money printers. The money printer lasts 5-7 years and pays for itself in 1-3. That's why companies keep building them.
